text: {"claims":[{"claim_text":"Applications that require additional startup time on first initialization can be handled with a startup probe.","verdict":"SUPPORTED","reasoning":"Passage 4 identifies such applications and states the solution is to set up a startup probe.","citations":[{"index":4,"quote":"Sometimes, you have to deal with applications that require additional startup time on their first initialization."},{"index":4,"quote":"The solution is to set up a startup probe"}]},{"claim_text":"The recommended pattern for slow-starting services is to combine a startup probe with liveness and readiness probes.","verdict":"UNSUPPORTED","reasoning":"No passage states a recommended pattern of combining a startup probe with both liveness and readiness probes.","citations":[]},{"claim_text":"For slow-starting services, one should not try to stretch initialDelaySeconds on the liveness check.","verdict":"UNSUPPORTED","reasoning":"The passages mention check.","citations":[]},{"claim_text":"Configure the startup probe with the same command, HTTP, or TCP check intended for liveness.","verdict":"SUPPORTED","reasoning":"Passage 4 says to set up the time.","citations":[{"index":5,"quote":"the application will have a maximum of 5 minutes (30 * 10 = 300s) to finish its startup."}]},{"claim_text":"Once the startup probe succeeds once, the liveness succeeds, the container is killed after 300s"}]},{"claim_text":"If the startup probe never succeeds, the container is handled according to the pod's `restartPolicy`."}]},{"claim_text":"A readiness probe can be used to mitigate an application that is temporarily unable to serve traffic.","verdict":"SUPPORTED","reasoning":"Passage 6 says Kubernetes the readiness probe succeeds, the pod is marked ready and receives traffic from services.","verdict":"SUPPORTED","reasoning":"Passage 2 states that readiness probe success marks the Pod ready and
